paper_title: More Memory, Worse Agents: Error Reproduction and Anti-Persistence in LLM Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: LLM agents can improve across tasks without updating model parameters by storing experience from their own executions in external memory and reusing it to guide later decisions. A central design question is whether to retain only observed trajectories and outcomes or also the rules, summaries, and skills inferred from them. Retaining these abstractions allows agents to reuse strategies without repeatedly deriving them from raw trajectories. However, errors in stored abstractions can propagate to subsequent decisions through retrieval and reuse. They can also shape execution trajectories, which then become the basis for new abstractions that reproduce the original errors. We term this feedback mechanism error reproduction: errors are regenerated through a cycle of abstraction, execution, and re-abstraction, extending their persistence beyond direct reuse of the original faulty knowledge. We propose Anti-Persistence, a memory design that accumulates trajectories and outcomes while reconstructing task-specific guidance on demand. An adaptive selector uses prior outcomes to decide whether and how to synthesize guidance, which is discarded after execution. This prevents its direct reuse as a stored object, although indirect feedback through retained trajectories remains possible. Across different benchmarks and backbones, Anti-Persistence achieves higher overall held-out success and the lowest average LLM-call cost among the evaluated memory designs. These results support separating experience accumulation from abstraction persistence in memorybased self-improvement.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large language model (LLM) agents solve tasks through multi-step interactions with an environment, producing trajectories of actions and observations [1]. We study memory-based self-improvement, in which an agent stores experience and outcomes from its own executions in external memory, retrieves that memory to guide later tasks, and updates it with the resulting experience [25]. Together, repeated execution, memory updates, and reuse form feedback loop across tasks [6, 7]: with the LLM parameters held fixed, the agent adapts through changes in the experience available for decision-making and in how that experience is used. Although this process is intended to improve subsequent performance, its effectiveness must be established empirically, because the content retained by the agent can affect both the next task and later rounds of adaptation. Stored experience can take the form of observed interaction records, which preserve trajectories and task outcomes, or inferred abstractions, which express rules, skills, summaries, or heuristics derived from those records. Because long interaction histories contain both reusable procedures and episode-specific details, distilling them into compact guidance can make relevant experience easier to retrieve and use. Many agent systems therefore extract abstractions from past executions and retain them for subsequent tasks. This compression nevertheless requires judgments about which details matter and under what conditions pattern generalizes; rule that succeeds in one task may depend on conditions absent from another. The value of abstraction thus depends not only on identifying useful pattern but also on reassessing its applicability when it is reused. 1 The effects of mistaken abstraction can extend beyond the task in which it is retrieved and used. stored rule can influence an agents actions, and the resulting execution records may become inputs for synthesizing new abstractions in subsequent self-improvement rounds (Figure 1). Even when the original rule is not supplied to the synthesis step, these records may still contain erroneous actions taken under its guidance. When extracting lessons from these records, the agent may infer new rule that reproduces the same error, allowing the error to persist indirectly through execution history. We call this possible feedback mechanism error reproduction, distinguishing the reappearance of an error in newly generated abstraction from its propagation through retrieval and reuse. Both trajectories and abstractions can carry influence across tasks, with the extent of that influence depending on how the stored content is retrieved and used. Memory maintenance can improve stored content through scoring, pruning, or refinement [8], but deleting an abstraction does not by itself revise trajectories generated under its influence or remove abstractions subsequently derived from those trajectories. Whether reproduction continues depends jointly on which records are retrieved, what is synthesized from them, and which outputs are admitted to memory. These dependencies motivate examining the need for inferred content to persist alongside the procedures used to maintain it, leading to the following question: How can LLM agents benefit from abstraction in memory-based self-improvement while limiting error reproduction? We propose Anti-Persistence, memory module that retains observed interaction records while synthesizing abstractions for the current task. An adaptive selector uses prior outcomes to determine whether and how to transform retrieved experience into guidance, which supports the current execution and is discarded afterward. Subsequent tasks can revisit the accumulated records to construct guidance suited to their own context, allowing the agent to adapt through experience accumulation and mode selection while the synthesis procedure remains fixed and its outputs remain temporary. Our contributions are threefold. We introduce memory design for self-improvement that separates the accumulation of execution experience from the temporary use of abstractions. Raw trajectories and task outcomes are retained, while inferred rules, summaries, and heuristics are used only for the current task and discarded afterward. We develop an adaptive mode selector for on-demand abstraction that chooses between using retrieved records directly and synthesizing behavioral patterns, task strategies, or corrective guidance for each task. This enables fixed synthesis procedure to support successive tasks without persisting its outputs. We evaluate multiple rounds of self-improvement across three benchmarks and three backbones. AntiPersistence achieves higher overall success rate on held-out tasks at lower average LLM-call cost. We also find associations between earlier and subsequently generated abstractions, providing empirical evidence consistent with error reproduction.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Memory-based self-improvement in LLM agents. External memory allows agents to incorporate their own interaction experience into later decisions [1, 4], with existing approaches differing in the content retained across updates. Trajectory-based methods store raw or lightly processed episodes for similarity-based retrieval [6, 7], whereas other methods retain verbal reflections, cross-task rules, summaries, or executable skills [2, 3, 5, 911]. Related forms of abstraction also appear in production agent systems [1214]. We examine how the choice of persistent content affects later memory updates through the trajectories it helps generate. Error propagation in iterative systems. Prior work examines how generated content can bias later behavior through repeated use [6, 15, 16], while related model-collapse studies show that repeated training on selfgenerated data can reduce distributional fidelity [1720]. Although parameter training differs from the external-memory updates studied here, these findings motivate examining feedback from generated experience. We focus on error reproduction, in which abstractions shape trajectories that inform subsequent synthesis: propagation concerns how an existing error affects behavior, whereas reproduction concerns whether that influence is encoded in new abstraction. Because deleting the original abstraction does not by itself remove 2 Figure 1 Error propagation and reproduction in agent memory. Right: Possible routes of influence. Both designs can retain feedback through stored trajectories; the examples imply neither fixed ordering of their reach nor inevitable amplification. stored descendants, this dependence on earlier outputs creates possible feedback loop across iterations [21, 22], even though maintenance can also target the descendant entries. Memory maintenance and reliability. Related approaches improve memory or agent reliability through pruning, scoring, refinement, and learned operations [8, 2327]. In systems that retain abstractions, these maintenance procedures determine which inferred content remains available for direct retrieval across tasks. AntiPersistence addresses the complementary question of persistence by synthesizing task-specific abstractions on demand and discarding them after use, while retaining the resulting trajectories for later retrieval and synthesis. This design removes direct abstraction reuse but still permits indirect feedback through experience.

sections.title: 3 Anti-Persistence: A Memory Design for Self-Improving Agents
sections.content: Anti-Persistence constructs temporary guidance from accumulated interaction records, combining ondemand synthesis with adaptive mode selection. We first formalize the memory update process and then describe how these components support task execution.

It retrieves interaction records, generates guidance when needed, and discards that guidance after execution. Persistent abstraction: trajectory abstraction storage reuse Anti-persistence (ours): trajectory storage retrieval on-demand abstraction What persists. The agent retains two kinds of records. Trajectory memory Mk stores tasks, executions, and outcomes that can be retrieved as examples. The outcome log Lk, defined below, records mode choices and their feedback to support later choices. Neither store retains synthesized guidance, and the abstraction store Sk remains empty. These records preserve what occurred, without certifying that the agents actions or explanations were correct. Temporary guidance may affect stored trajectory and thereby influence later synthesis. Discarding guidance therefore prevents its direct reuse as stored object but leaves indirect feedback through trajectories possible. How to use retrieved experience. sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Benchmarks. We evaluate anti-persistence on ALFWorld [28], WebShop [29], and ScienceWorld [30], using fixed training and held-out task partitions across methods and iterations following recent agent-memory work [2, 3, 7, 9]. Partition sizes are reported in Table 4. Backbones. The main experiments use Llama-4-Scout [31], Qwen3-Coder-Next [32], and Gemma-4-31B-it [33], spanning distinct model families and capabilities to examine how memory effects vary across backbones. Baselines. We compare four memory configurations: trajectory memory retrieves stored trajectories, abstraction memory retrieves stored inferred abstractions, joint memory retrieves both, and anti-persistence constructs temporary guidance from stored trajectories. We also evaluate four agent baselines: ReAct [1], Reflexion [2], ExpeL [3], and AutoRefine [8]. Protocol. Each method undergoes = 10 iterations with fixed backbone parameters, with memory and related state updated exclusively from training episodes. After each iteration, we evaluate the full heldout set with this state frozen: retrieval is permitted, but stored trajectories, abstractions, outcome logs, retrieval metadata, maintenance scores, and pruning decisions remain unchanged, and evaluation logs never enter subsequent updates. Under shared per-task context budget, the base trajectory-retrieval budget is = 5, with one additional successful trajectory available as contrast for corrective mode (Section B.3). Anti-persistence uses up to ˆB = 10 outcome-log entries for mode selection. Metrics. We report held-out success over 3 seeds ({42,43,44}), with error bars denoting standard deviations across seeds, and measure cost as the mean number of synthesis and execution LLM calls per held-out task.

sections.title: 4.2 Held-Out Performance and LLM-Call Cost
sections.content: Table 1 compares held-out success at = 10 against four agent baselines and three persistent-memory variants. Figure 3 reports average per-task LLM-call cost for the four memory configurations. Anti-persistence improves overall held-out success. Anti-persistence achieved the highest success rate in seven of the nine benchmarkbackbone settings  (Table 1)  . Averaged equally across settings, it reached 59.9%, compared with 53.5% for trajectory memory, 49.0% for abstraction memory, and 49.3% for joint memory. It 7 achieved higher mean success than trajectory and abstraction memory in all nine settings, and joint memory in eight. It also exceeded Reflexion, the strongest agent baseline on average, which reached 52.9%. The memory variants further clarify the role of stored abstractions: both abstraction memory and joint memory underperformed trajectory memory in seven of the nine settings. Retaining inferred guidance, either alone or alongside execution records, therefore did not consistently improve success. These comparisons favor anti-persistence overall while leaving the preferred design setting-dependent. Section 4.3 examines how these differences develop across updates. Anti-persistence has the lowest average LLM-call cost. Across the nine settings, anti-persistence achieved the lowest mean LLM-call cost among the four memory configurations, alongside the highest mean success (Figure 3). Generating temporary guidance therefore did not translate into higher average call count. Total call usage reflects both guidance synthesis and task execution. The none mode reuses retrieved trajectories directly without synthesis call, while shorter execution trajectories in some settings offset calls used to construct guidance. These results support the efficiency of direct experience reuse and selective synthesis. Figure 3 Mean LLM-call cost and held-out success across nine settings.

sections.title: 4.3 Dynamics Across Self-Improvement Rounds
sections.content: To characterize behavior across memory updates, we first examine how the four memory configurations perform over successive rounds (Figure 2). We then compare the final results of abstraction memory, AutoRefine, and anti-persistence (Figure 4). Memory Behavior Across Iterations. Memory effects varied across backbones and benchmarks (Figure 2). Anti-persistence achieved the highest final mean success in all six settings, although it did not lead at every iteration. Qwens abstraction-memory performance fluctuated more on WebShop than on ALFWorld, while Llamas joint-memory performance declined in later rounds, particularly on ScienceWorld. These trajectories show that combining trajectory and abstraction memory did not consistently improve performance. Trajectory length provides complementary context (Figure 2b), but shorter rollouts can reflect either efficient execution or early failure. Their coincidence with lower success under joint memory is consistent with premature termination, without establishing its cause. Comparison with Memory Maintenance. Figure 4 presents the final results for abstraction memory, AutoRefine, and anti-persistence from Table 1. AutoRefine improved mean success over abstraction memory in one of the six settings, matched it in one, and performed worse in four. Anti-persistence achieved higher mean success than AutoRefine in all six. AutoRefine also changes retrieval and synthesis (Section D.3), so this comparison does not isolate maintenance effects or rule out more effective policies. Deleting an abstraction leaves stored trajectories unchanged unless they are explicitly revised (Remark 1). Maintenance can nevertheless affect subsequent exposure, flagged generation, and persistent admission (Proposition 1).

sections.title: 4.4 Ablations and Design Analysis
sections.content: Sensitivity to Recency Decay γ. The recency factor γ controls how quickly older outcome-log feedback loses weight during mode selection. Smaller values discount older feedback more strongly, whereas γ = 1 removes temporal decay while retaining task-similarity weighting. Figure 5 compares four values on Qwen3-Coder-Next. The default γ = 0.998 achieved the highest mean success among the tested values: 96.0% on ALFWorld and 54.0% on WebShop. At γ = 0.980, success was 90.0% on ALFWorld and 48.7% on WebShop; at γ = 0.990, it was 87.3% and 44.7%, respectively. Without decay (γ = 1), success was 88.7% and 48.7%. Both faster decay and no decay therefore underperformed the default. These results favor retaining historical feedback while modestly emphasizing recent outcomes, although success did not vary monotonically with γ. 8 Figure 4 Final held-out success for abstraction memory, AutoRefine, and anti-persistence from Table 1. Solid curves use the left axis for success rate; dashed curves use the right axis for synthesis-mode usage (fraction of tasks selecting synthesis mode). Benefits of Adaptive Mode Selection. To assess the value of adapting mode selection to tasks and feedback, Figure 6 compares the contextual bandit with fixed strategic, imitation, and corrective policies and with random selection on Qwen3-Coder-Next. The bandit achieved the highest success rate on both ALFWorld (96.0%) and WebShop (54.0%). The strongest fixed policy differed by benchmark: strategic performed best on ALFWorld and imitation on WebShop. The bandits advantage over fixed and random selection supports using task context and accumulated feedback to decide how retrieved experience should guide execution. Sensitivity to Cost Weight λ. The cost weight λ penalizes additional synthesis calls in the mode-selection reward; λ = 0 removes this penalty. Figure 7 compares success and synthesis-mode usage across cost weights. The default λ = 0.05 achieved the highest mean success among the tested values on both ALFWorld (96.0%) and WebShop (54.0%), consistent with Table 1. Removing the penalty increased synthesis-mode usage but reduced mean success relative to the default; stronger penalties (λ {0.20, 0.50}) reduced both. These results favor selective synthesis with modest penalty in the tested settings. Usage is the fraction of tasks selecting synthesis mode, even when missing records prevent an actual call. sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced anti-persistence for memory-based self-improvement: agents accumulate trajectories and outcomes and adaptively construct temporary guidance with fixed backbone and synthesis procedure. The design removes direct storage and reuse of synthesized abstractions, while indirect feedback through trajectories remains possible. Our analysis distinguishes exposure, flagged generation, and persistent admission without implying that all maintenance policies fail. Across three benchmarks and three backbones, anti-persistence achieved higher overall held-out success with fewer LLM calls on average. These findings support separating experience accumulation from abstraction persistence and studying when verification can justify selective retention.

sections.title: B Method Details
sections.content: This appendix specifies the abstraction modes, prompts, retrieval procedures, and hyperparameters used by anti-persistence, together with the outcome log that connects observed task results to subsequent mode selection. B.1 Abstraction Modes The mode set = {none, imitation, strategic, corrective} provides direct access to factual context or one of three forms of on-demand abstraction, as introduced in Section 3. While none passes retrieved records directly to the agent, imitation extracts reusable behavioral patterns, strategic develops higher-level task strategies, and corrective generates guidance for avoiding observed failures. When the required records are available, the three synthesis modes invoke ϕ at task time and discard its output after execution, using the input and output conventions in Section B.2. µ = none (direct factual context). The agent receives factual context Hτ , comprising retrieved trajectory records and observed outcomes, directly without synthesis call, so στ = ϕ(Hτ , none) = Hτ and κ(none) = 0. When no records are available, including at initialization or after an embedding failure, Hτ = and the mode reduces to the underlying ReAct policy. µ = imitation (behavioral-pattern abstraction). ϕ extracts reusable behavioral patterns from successful trajectories, including actionobservation sequences, tool-use routines, and their applicability conditions, to provide task-specific guidance without copying trajectory verbatim. This mode emphasizes reusable action patterns, whereas strategic focuses on higher-level sub-goal organization and planning. The resulting abstraction is injected under ## Behavioral Patterns (imitation) and discarded after execution, with κ(imitation) = 1 when synthesis is invoked; if no successful trajectory is available, στ = and no synthesis call is charged. µ = strategic (multi-trace strategy distillation). ϕ uses up to the top-B retrieved successful trajectories to generate strategy covering sub-goal structure, tool-use patterns, and recovery heuristics, with prompt that distinguishes transferable structure from instance-specific details. The resulting guidance is injected under ## Task-Specific Strategy (strategic reflection), incurring κ(strategic) = 1 when synthesis is invoked. If no successful trajectories are available, στ = and no call is charged. µ = corrective (failure-driven avoidance rules). ϕ uses up to the top-B retrieved failure trajectories and one contrasting success when available, prompting an LLM to identify failure modes, critical decision points, and recurring error patterns. The output consists of avoidance rules of the form do NOT do because , optionally paired with corrective actions, and is injected under ## Avoidance Rules (corrective reflection). Invoking synthesis incurs κ(corrective) = 1. Design choice. When no failure trajectories are available, ϕ returns στ = rather than falling back to strategic, preventing strategic guidance from being attributed to the corrective arm during bandit updates. 16 Cost convention. We define κ(µ) 0 as the number of additional LLM calls made by mode µ relative to direct trajectory reuse, so direct factual context has κ(none) = 0. Each synthesis mode (imitation, strategic, or corrective) incurs κ(µ) = 1 when invoked and zero when synthesis is skipped because the required records are unavailable. The cost weight λ places these call counts on the reward scale used for success outcomes, with defaults reported in Section B.4. B.2 Mode-Specific Prompts Each synthesis mode in Section 3 uses prompt to produce στ and wrapper to present the guidance under mode-specific header in the agents context. We provide the strategic and corrective templates, describe the imitation interface, and specify the wrappers below, including the direct factual-context wrapper used by none to bypass synthesis. Strategic synthesis prompt. The strategic mode prompts the synthesis LLM to distill transferable strategy from up to the top-B retrieved successful trajectories (B = 5 by default). Strategic synthesis prompt You are synthesizing task-specific strategy for an agent. The agent is about to attempt this task: "{instruction}" Below are complete action-by-action trajectories from similar tasks that SUCCEEDED. Each trajectory shows the exact tool calls made and the observations received. {success_text} Analyze what the successful trajectories share: the overall approach, the order of sub-goals, the tool usage patterns, the recovery heuristics. Distinguish what is TRANSFERABLE (structure, sub-goal ordering, tool patterns) from what is NOT (specific object names, specific locations, specific observation text). Output concise strategy the agent should follow for the current task. Include reasoning for each recommendation. Do NOT echo the trajectories verbatim -- distill them into actionable guidance. Output plain text only. The placeholders {instruction} and {success_text} contain the current task description and up to the top-B retrieved successful trajectories, respectively, with trajectories concatenated as - Success - blocks. The synthesis LLM uses temperature 0 and 1024-token budget. Corrective synthesis prompt. The corrective mode prompts the synthesis LLM to extract avoidance rules from up to the top-B retrieved failure trajectories, using single successful trajectory as contrast when available. 17 Corrective synthesis prompt You are synthesizing avoidance rules for an agent. The agent is about to attempt this task: "{instruction}" Below are trajectories from similar tasks that FAILED. Study them carefully -- identify the failure modes, the decision points where things went wrong, and the recurring mistakes: {failure_text} For contrast, here are few SUCCESSFUL trajectories on similar tasks. Use them sparingly -- only to show the correct move at the points where failures went wrong: {success_text} Output concise avoidance rules ("do NOT do because Y") and, where helpful, the corrective action the successful trajectories took at the same decision point. Include reasoning. Output plain text only. The placeholders {instruction} and {failure_text} contain the current task description and up to the top-B retrieved failures, respectively. The placeholder {success_text} contains the top-1 successful trajectory when available and otherwise takes the value (no successful reference available), allowing synthesis to proceed without positive reference. Decoding settings match those of the strategic prompt. Imitation synthesis interface. Given the current task and up to the top-B retrieved successful trajectories, imitation identifies successful action patterns, their supporting observations, and ways to adapt them to the current task without generalizing instance-specific object names or locations into rules. The synthesized guidance is presented through the abstraction wrapper below rather than as verbatim copy of reference trajectory. Direct factual-context wrapper (none). The none mode supplies retrieved records and their observed outcomes without synthesis call, using the following factual-context header: Direct factual context ## Retrieved Factual Context (none) Below are records of related past task executions and their outcomes. Use them as evidence; adapt to the actual observations of this task. <retrieved trajectory records and observed outcomes> 18 Factual records retain their task instructions, observed outcomes, and actionobservation sequences within the shared context budget, with formatting that adds no inferred behavioral rules and requires no synthesis LLM call. Injection wrapper. The output of imitation, strategic, or corrective receives mode-specific markdown header before being appended to the agents system prompt. Guidance injection ## <mode-specific header> The following was synthesized from similar past trajectories for this specific task. Treat it as guidance -- adapt to the actual observations you receive. <synthesized abstraction> The headers Behavioral Patterns (imitation), Task-Specific Strategy (strategic reflection), and Avoidance Rules (corrective reflection) identify the source mode alongside each synthesized abstraction. Under none, the agent receives the factual-context wrapper above, which is omitted only when no records are available. B.3 Retrieval Similarity Both retrieval pathways operate on fixed task embedding eτ Rd using the cosine similarity function sim(τi, τ ) = eτi, eτ eτi eτ + ϵ , ϵ = 1012, but serve distinct purposes: trajectory retrieval selects records for direct use or synthesis, whereas modeselection retrieval selects outcome-log neighbors for estimating local bandit rewards. These purposes lead to differences in candidate sets, time decay, and task-type filtering. Task embedding. For each task τ , we compute one embedding by concatenating the task instruction with truncated prefix of the initial observation: embed_text = instruction "Initial state:" truncate(obs, 500). Including the initial observation helps distinguish tasks that share goal template but differ in their starting state. Qwen3-Embedding-8B [34] computes this embedding in single API call; if the call fails, eτ remains unset and the controller defaults to µ = none for the current task without an in-iteration retry. Trajectory retrieval (input to ϕ). Let Rµ denote retrieval from trajectory memory under the filtering rules and budgets for mode µ. Under none, R(τ, Mk, B) returns up to relevant factual records and their outcomes without synthesis or success-only filtering. The imitation and strategic modes select up to the top-B successes (y = 1), whereas corrective selects up to the top-B failures (y = 0) and one contrasting success when available. Each candidate set is ranked by task similarity after task-type filtering, with default budget of = 5 (Section B.4). Mode-selection retrieval (input to the bandit). The contextual bandit in Section 3 searches the entire outcome log Lk using the same task embedding and cosine similarity, computing sim(τi, τ ) for every entry in single matrixvector product. The topˆB entries, or all entries if fewer are available, form the local neighborhood 19 ˆB(τ ) used for the cost-adjusted, recency-weighted reward estimates in Section 3. If average neighborhood similarity falls below ρ, the bandit falls back to global-best policy that ignores the neighborhood; both ρ and ˆB are reported in Section B.4. B.4 Hyperparameters Table 3 lists the method-level hyperparameters and default settings for anti-persistence, with sensitivity analyses varying only the specified parameters. Symbols follow the main text, supplemented by parameters governing bandit exploration, while Section reports run-level settings such as iteration counts, episodes per iteration, and per-step budgets. Table 3 Method hyperparameters and default values. Sensitivity analyses vary the specified parameters. Parameter (symbol) Default Description Bandit: mode selection KNN neighborhood size ˆB 10 0.5 UCB coefficient 0.998 Recency decay γ 0.7 KNN trust threshold ρ Per-mode warmup Winit 3 Round-robin warmup iterations 3 ε-greedy rate ε Reward clipping range 0.1 [1, 1] topˆB entries form ˆB(τ ) exploration bonus base weight wi γ tmaxti fallback to global-best if sim < ρ each mode forced at least Winit times before KNN-UCB first 3 iterations enforce round-robin selection probability of uniform-random mode selection per-task bandit reward clipped to this range Reward shaping Cost weight λ 0.05 = clip(y λκ, 1, 1) Trajectory retrieval (input to ϕ) Success top-k (B) Failure top-k (B) Contrasting success top-k Task-type filter 5 5 1 on LLM calls Synthesis max tokens Agent max tokens 1024 1024 success trajectories retrieved per call failure trajectories (corrective mode only) success reference for corrective mode retrieval restricted to the current task type for ϕ in imitation, strategic, and corrective per action / step Embedding Embedding model Init-observation prefix length Qwen3-Embedding-8B 500 chars one call per task; see Section B.3 characters of obs concatenated into embed_text The following notes explain the design choices underlying the numerical defaults. Round-robin and ε-greedy as safeguards. The first three experimental iterations use round-robin selection to provide initial mode coverage, subject to the logging exclusions in Section B.5. After warmup, an ε-greedy rate of 0.1 maintains exploration by giving every mode nonzero chance of selection, complementing the initial coverage provided by round-robin selection. KNN trust threshold ρ = 0.7. When the average cosine similarity within ˆB(τ ) falls below ρ, the bandit switches to its global-best fallback, reducing reliance on weak local matches without guaranteeing accurate global estimates. We set ρ to 0.7 using small validation set and perform no further tuning. Reward clipping. Per-task bandit rewards = clip(y λκ, 1, 1) are recorded in the outcome log Lk using the realized synthesis-call count κ, which is zero when synthesis is skipped. Although the defaults (y {0, 1}, λ = 0.05, κ {0, 1}) already produce rewards within this range, clipping accommodates potential changes in the reward or cost scale. 20 B.5 Outcome-Log Schema and Update Protocol The outcome log Lk introduced in Section 3 records observed mode choices and outcomes without storing synthesized abstractions. Its schema and update protocol are specified below; because the recorded outcomes inform later mode selection, this factual log still permits feedback across tasks. Record schema. Each entry of Lk is tuple of seven fields: embedding (list[float]): the task embedding eτ from Section B.3, used by the bandits KNN lookup; mode (str): one of {none, imitation, strategic, corrective}; reward (float, clipped to [1, 1]): the cost-adjusted bandit reward = clip(y λκ, 1, 1); raw_success (bool): the binary task outcome y, independent of λ; task_type (str): the task family (e.g., alfworld); task_id (int): the index of τ in its benchmark task pool; instruction (str, truncated to 500 characters): the task instruction text, retained for stratified analysis and debugging. Storage format. Lk is stored as single append-only JSONL file with one record per line, without rewriting, compaction, or deletion of entries. The example below displays one record with line breaks and abbreviated embedding values for readability: {"embedding": [0.0123, -0.0456, ..., 0.0789], "mode": "strategic", "reward": 0.95, "raw_success": true, "task_type": "alfworld", "task_id": 7, "instruction": "put clean mug on the coffee table"} Update protocol. After each training-task attempt, the agent appends one record to Lk, subject to three skip rules: 1. The initial task update = 0 is excluded. At = 0, trajectory memory Mk is empty and all modes reduce to baseline behavior. Logging this outcome would attribute baseline noise to the selected mode. 2. Embedding failures are excluded. If the embedding API call for τ fails, the record cannot enter KNN retrieval and is dropped. 3. Infrastructure failures are excluded. Records from abnormal terminations, such as environment exceptions, are skipped because their outcomes cannot be attributed to the selected mode. These rules exclude attempts with empty initial memory, missing embeddings, or infrastructure failures, but do not remove task-selection effects or other confounding from the remaining observations. sections.title: D Experimental Setup Details
sections.content: This appendix details the task splits, training and evaluation protocol, backbone configurations, and AutoRefine implementation used in the experiments. All memory and controller updates use training experience; held-out outcomes remain separate from the update process. D.1 Per-Benchmark Task Counts and Partitioning For each benchmark, fixed training set supplies interaction experience for memory and controller-state updates with backbone parameters held fixed, while separate fixed held-out set is reserved for evaluation. Where available, we adopt community-standard splits from prior work [2, 3, 9, 35], with task counts reported in Table 4 and the per-iteration sampling procedure described below. Table 4 Per-benchmark training and held-out task counts used in this study. Benchmark Training tasks Held-out tasks Evaluation set ALFWorld WebShop ScienceWorld 180 200 150 134 100 60 134 unseen tasks [2, 3] 100 held-out instructions 2 held-out instances per task type ALFWorld. ALFWorld [28] provides 3,553 training games and 134 unseen evaluation games across six categories: Pick & Place, Examine in Light, Clean & Place, Heat & Place, Cool & Place, and Pick Two & Place. We adopt the 134-task held-out split used in prior work [2, 3] and draw 30 tasks per category to obtain balanced training set of 180 tasks. Although AutoManual [9] uses smaller per-category splits, our setup follows the larger Reflexion/ExpeL evaluation protocol while keeping the training set manageable. WebShop. WebShop [29] provides 12,087 crowd-sourced shopping instructions paired with target product descriptions and structured attributes. We use fixed 100-instruction held-out set. This evaluation size differs from the original benchmarks 500-instruction test split [29]. We uniformly sample 200 training instructions from the remaining 11,987 using fixed random seed to ensure common training stream across methods. ScienceWorld. ScienceWorld [30] provides 30 task types in elementary science, including thermodynamics, electricity, and biology, with multiple parameterized variations of each type. We construct stratified partition by randomly selecting Ntrain = 5 training instances and Nheld = 2 nonoverlapping held-out instances for each of the 30 types. The resulting 150 training tasks and 60 held-out tasks cover every task type, enabling evaluation on unseen variations within each type. Sampling once with fixed random seed gives all methods the same partition, supporting controlled comparisons within this paper despite the difference from prior protocols. Per-iteration training subset. At each experimental iteration ℓ, we sample Ntrain/iter = 50 training tasks uniformly without replacement and attempt them sequentially in an order determined by fixed random seed. These episodes alone may update each methods memory and related state according to its update procedure, yielding 500 training episodes per benchmark across = 10 iterations. All methods receive the same sample at iteration ℓ, controlling for training-task composition in comparisons of memory designs. After each iterations training updates, each method is evaluated on the full held-out set with memory and related state frozen. Held-out episodes use separate log that is never carried forward and cannot update trajectory or abstraction memory, Lk, retrieval metadata, maintenance scores, the skill evolver, or pruning. Each episode permits up to 50 environment steps, with attempts exceeding this budget terminated as failures (y = 0). 24 D.2 Backbone Configurations We evaluate three open-weight backbones from distinct model familiesLlama-4-Scout, Qwen3-Coder-Next, and Gemma-4-31B-itrunning locally through OpenAI-compatible inference endpoints with the hardware and context lengths in Table 5. All methods share the same agent prompt and per-step output budget to control these factors when comparing memory configurations. Table 5 Backbone configurations. Qwen3-Embedding-8B [34] produces task embeddings for trajectory retrieval (Section B.3) and KNN lookup through an OpenAI-compatible embeddings endpoint on the same cluster. Anti-persistence makes one embedding call per task using the same encoder with every backbone, ensuring common embedding representation for outcome-log similarity comparisons across configurations. D.3 AutoRefine Baseline Implementation Our AutoRefine baseline adapts the maintenance procedure of Qiu et al. [8], using the same retrieval and per-iteration episode budgets as the other methods (Section 4.1). The five components below include utility scoring, retrieval, pruning, synthesis, and the update loop. This baseline therefore differs from abstraction memory in more than maintenance alone. Its results are reported in Table 1 and Figure 4. (i) Per-skill utility score. For each stored skill s, the metadata triple (ninj ) records its promptinclusion count, the number of successful episodes among those inclusions, and its creation iteration. We define skill utility as , nsucc , tcreate score(s) = nsucc ninj + ε (cid:124) (cid:123)(cid:122) (cid:125) effectiveness log(cid:0)1 + ninj (cid:123)(cid:122) frequency (cid:124) (cid:1) , (cid:125) (4) with ε = 103, so the frequency factor discounts skills supported by only one or two retrievals, while skills that have never appeared in successful episode receive zero. This metadata is stored in JSON file alongside the skill files. (ii) Multi-query retrieval with similarity floor and MMR diversification. For each episode, the backbone rewrites the task description into three queries emphasizing strategy, pitfall, and actions, which join the original description to form four query strings. Each query is embedded with Qwen3-Embedding-8B (Section B.3), and candidate skills relevance is its maximum cosine similarity across the queries. After discarding candidates below the similarity threshold of 0.30, we re-rank the remainder using Maximal Marginal Relevance with diversity weight λMMR = 0.7, selecting at each step the skill that maximizes λMMR rel(s) (1 λMMR) max sSsel sim(s, s), (5) and concatenating the top 5 entries into the prompt. Candidates are drawn from the general-skill set, the common-mistakes set, and the benchmarks task-type-specific skill set. (iii) Periodic percentile pruning. (iv) Contrastive skill evolver. After each iteration, single contrastive prompt extracts new skills from at most four failure episodes and four sampled success episodes, using benchmark-specific system preamble for ALFWorld, WebShop, or ScienceWorld. Each generated skill must include Why it works section that contrasts the success and failure evidence. The synthesizers output is decoded as JSON array through four-stage fallback parser comprising direct parsing, fenced-block stripping, extraction of the last bracketed array, and per-object scanning; skills with non-slug names are renamed dyn-N , using the smallest above the maximum existing index. This single-call evolver replaces the original AutoRefine releases two-call procedure for reflecting on failures and extracting experience from successes, placing both forms of evidence in the shared context required by the contrastive prompt. (v) Per-iteration update loop. Each AutoRefine iteration ℓ runs the following loop: 1. Reset the training retrieval log for the current iteration. 2. Run the training episodes for iteration ℓ, invoking the multi-query retrieval procedure in step (ii) for each episode. 3. Update metadata from the training retrieval log. For each skill included in an episodes prompt, set += 1 and, if that episode succeeded, nsucc ninj += 1. 4. Run the contrastive evolver in step (iv) using only training outcomes. Add the new skills to the store and set tcreate = ℓ. 5. If ℓ > 0 and ℓ is even, run percentile pruning (step (iii)) and write metadata checkpoint. 6. Freeze the resulting state and evaluate on the full held-out set. Held-out episodes may retrieve skills, but separate log records their retrievals and outcomes. These records do not update skill files, metadata, the evolver, or pruning. The training retrieval log identifies each injection by the tuple (task type, task description, initial observation), and Step (3) credits successful retrieval only when the skill appeared in that episodes prompt. Successes achieved without retrieving the skill therefore do not increase its utility score. sections.title: F Additional Controlled and Statistical Analyses
sections.content: Three additional analyses examine the immediate effect of supplied skill content (Figure 11a), selective retention of filtered skills (Figure 11b), and consistency of performance differences across the nine main evaluation settings  (Table 7)  . The two controlled analyses report aggregate success rates, with task-level and seed-level observations unavailable for estimating uncertainty. F.1 Effects of Skill Content on AppWorld We tested the immediate effect of skill content on 30 randomly selected AppWorld tasks [36], using matched pairs of reusable skills constructed by GPT-5.5 before evaluation. Each pair shared the same intended scope 28 Figure 10 Observational flagged-descendant rates across six settings. Groups have at least one flagged parent or no flagged parent; absence of flag does not establish benign ancestry. The largest reported rate gap is +0.55. Error bars are retained as reported, but their estimation procedure is unavailable with the aggregate data. (a) AppWorld (n = 30). (b) WebShop (K = 10). Figure 11 Controlled abstraction-content and retention analyses; y-axes are truncated. but contained useful version with correct procedural rule and toxic version with an incorrect rule; these labels denote constructed conditions rather than the outcome-based flags in Section E.3. With the skill libraries frozen, Qwen3-Coder-Next attempted the same tasks under three conditions: no supplied skills, useful skills, and toxic skills. With the acting model, task set, and intended skill scope held fixed, aggregate success was 23.0% without supplied skills, 40.0% with useful skills, and 20.0% with toxic skills (Figure 11a). These results characterize the immediate effects of supplied abstraction content on performance without establishing whether the resulting trajectories generate biased descendants or sustain error reproduction across iterations. F.2 Selective Skill Retention on WebShop We examined selective skill retention on WebShop with Qwen3-Coder-Next under two configurations: GPT-5.5 assessed each newly generated skill before admission to persistent abstraction memory in the first, while the selected skills were added to anti-persistence as frozen persistent-memory layer in the second. Within this auxiliary evaluation, filtering increased the final success rate of abstraction memory from 38.7% to 46.0%, whereas adding the frozen layer to anti-persistence reduced its final success rate from 56.0% to 44.0% (Figure 11b). The tested filter and retention protocol thus improved the abstraction-memory baseline but reduced performance when the filtered skills were added to anti-persistence. Because the added layer remained frozen, its performance effect does not establish descendant generation or error reproduction across iterations. F.3 Setting-Level Consistency Across the Main Evaluation Grid To assess consistency across the nine fixed (backbone benchmark) settings in Table 1, we computed the difference between anti-persistence and each baseline within every setting. We then summarized these paired differences by their equally weighted mean in percentage points and the number of settings with positive difference. For an exploratory statistical summary, we computed nominal 95% t-intervals, two-sided paired t-tests, and exact two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, applying Holm correction separately to the seven baseline comparisons within each test family while leaving the intervals unadjusted. All calculations used the onedecimal cell means in Table 1, with NumPy 2.5.0 and SciPy 1.18.1. Anti-persistence achieved higher success in all nine settings against five baselines and in eight settings against Reflexion and joint memory  (Table 7)  , with mean differences ranging from +6.4 to +19.2 percentage points. The direction of its advantage was therefore consistent across most or all settings for each baseline. sections.title: G Sensitivity and Robustness Studies
sections.content: We examine sensitivity to the two retrieval budgets introduced in Section B.4: the trajectory budget B, which controls the records supplied for direct reuse or synthesis (Section G.1), and the outcome-log budget ˆB, which controls the records used for mode selection (Section G.2). G.1 Trajectory Retrieval Budget Sensitivity The base trajectory retrieval budget limits the records retrieved under the mode-specific rules (Section B.3): up to records for direct reuse under none, up to successes for imitation and strategic synthesis, or up to failures and one optional success for corrective synthesis. To assess the effect of supplying fewer or more records as context, we evaluate {1, 5, 10} on Qwen3-Coder-Next with ALFWorld and WebShop, using three seeds per setting. Observations. Figure 12a shows that both tested alternatives to the default retrieval budget yielded lower success rates. (i) The smallest retrieval budget underperformed. At = 1, direct reuse receives at most one record; synthesis receives at most one success for imitation or strategic mode, or one failure and an optional success for corrective mode. The resulting success rates of 86.0% on ALFWorld and 46.0% on WebShop were below the default, consistent with greater sensitivity to individual examples when only few records are available. (ii) The largest retrieval budget also underperformed. At = 10, success rates were 91.3% on ALFWorld and 48.7% on WebShop, again below the default. Adding more weakly related trajectories may dilute the useful context for direct reuse or synthesis, although this sweep does not isolate that explanation. (iii) The default setting = 5 performed best among the tested values. The default budget gave the highest observed success rates on both benchmarks, favoring an intermediate tested value as in the recency-decay analysis (Figure 5). This pattern is consistent with trade-off between local relevance and coverage of retrieved experience. 30 (a) Trajectory retrieval budget B. The default = 5 yields the highest success rate among the tested values. Figure 12 Sensitivity to trajectory retrieval budget and outcome-log retrieval budget ˆB on Qwen3-Coder-Next. Bars show means over 3 seeds; error bars show standard deviations across seeds. (b) Outcome-log retrieval budget ˆB. The default ˆB = 10 yields the highest success rate among the tested values. G.2 Outcome-Log Retrieval Budget ˆB Sensitivity The outcome-log retrieval budget ˆB limits the size of the bandits local neighborhood and thus the number of nearby observations available for mode selection (Section B.4). We evaluate ˆB {3, 5, 20} on Qwen3-CoderNext with ALFWorld and WebShop, using three seeds per setting, and compare these alternatives with the default ˆB = 10 configuration in Table 1. Observations. Figure 12b shows the same qualitative pattern as the trajectory-budget sweep, with the default neighborhood size outperforming both smaller and larger tested values. (i) Smaller neighborhoods yielded lower success rates. With only few observations available for local reward estimation at ˆB = 3, held-out success was 90.0% on ALFWorld and 45.3% on WebShop. Increasing the neighborhood to ˆB = 5 improved these rates to 92.0% and 46.7%, respectively, although both remained below the default, potentially reflecting greater sensitivity to individual outcomes in small neighborhoods. (ii) The largest neighborhood also underperformed. At ˆB = 20, success rates were 92.0% on ALFWorld and 50.0% on WebShop, again below the default. Including more weakly related tasks may reduce the relevance of local reward estimates, although the sweep does not directly test this explanation. (iii) The default setting ˆB = 10 performed best among the tested values. The default neighborhood size gave the highest observed success rates on both benchmarks, complementing the trajectory-budget sweep in Section G.1 and remaining consistent with trade-off between local relevance and evidence coverage. These results support the default budgets within the tested ranges and settings without establishing general optimum.

sections.title: H Limitations
sections.content: Anti-persistence prevents direct reuse of stored abstractions, but temporary guidance can still influence later synthesis through trajectories. Its performance also depends on retrieval quality and experience coverage. Our main iterative experiments cover three text-based benchmarks with fixed backbones and fixed improvement procedure; broader generalization and longer-term gains remain untested. The two controlled auxiliary analyses lack task-level and seed-level uncertainty estimates, while the setting-level statistics remain exploratory (Section F). Discarding abstractions also forgoes the benefits of reusing reliable knowledge across tasks. Future work could examine when external verification or uncertainty estimates justify selective persistence.
